name: Pretrichial brow lift

card.summary: A surgical brow lift through an incision at the front hairline that raises the brows without lengthening the forehead and can shorten a high forehead, giving a more youthful, open upper face.
card.note: Surgical procedure; scarring, numbness and revision are possible.

quick.overview:
A pretrichial brow lift raises drooping or low brows through an incision placed just in front of the hairline. Because the scalp is not pulled back, it does not raise the hairline, which makes it a choice for people who already have a high forehead.

Surgeons describe it as rejuvenating the upper face and easy to combine with eyelid surgery. A 2004 chart review of an endoscopic pretrichial variant judged it effective in selected patients [3], and a 46-patient series with eyelid surgery reported satisfaction scores of about 3.2 of 4 [5].
quick.how: The surgeon makes an incision along the front hairline, lifts the brow and forehead tissue, removes a strip of skin and closes it; scalp advancement can be combined to shorten the forehead [2]. It is often done together with upper eyelid surgery [5].
quick.risks: Reported issues include asymmetry, numbness, scarring, hair loss at the incision and bruising. A comparison of 72 patients found complication rates similar between endoscopic and pretrichial lifts, with greater brow elevation after the endoscopic route [4]. Revision rates are said to be highest after hairline lifts [9].

lead: A pretrichial brow lift is an open brow-lifting operation in which the incision runs along the front edge of the hairline (pretrichial means in front of the hair). Surgeons use it to raise a low or drooping brow, soften forehead creases and open the eyes, particularly in patients with a high hairline because it avoids lifting the hairline further.[3][3]

For appearance, the approach can also shorten a long forehead: one review notes that a long forehead may make the face look disproportionate and older, and surgical options for correction exist.[7] A 2018 article describes combining scalp advancement with the pretrichial lift to reduce forehead length and temporal recession.[2]
Published evidence is mostly retrospective case series and comparisons. StatPearls describes the technique and its role in patients with droopy-eye complaints.[8]

chain: Higher brows, shorter forehead proportion, more open eyes
angle.text: The lift elevates the brow and, with scalp advancement, reduces forehead height. It gives a more open, youthful upper face without pushing the hairline back.

paras: Brow lift types include endoscopic, coronal, direct, mid-forehead, temporal, internal and pretrichial approaches.[9] The pretrichial technique places the incision at the hairline so that forehead skin is removed rather than scalp, avoiding a raised hairline.[8]

Brow ptosis can worsen eyelid hooding by pushing skin down over the upper lid, and the lift is combined with blepharoplasty for that reason.[5] StatPearls notes that patients may not realise brow position contributes to an aged look.[8] For long foreheads, patients were grouped by forehead length and treated accordingly.[7]

In a 46-patient series of pretrichial lift plus upper blepharoplasty, mean brow lift at 3 months ranged from about 1.1 to 1.9 mm depending on location, minor complications occurred in 15.2% and satisfaction averaged about 3.2 of 4.[5] In a 72-patient comparison, ecchymosis, numbness, hematoma, scarring and alopecia did not differ significantly between endoscopic and pretrichial groups; early brow height change was 21% endoscopic versus 13% pretrichial.[4]

A 2004 chart review of endoscopic pretrichial brow lifts concluded the technique was effective in properly selected patients and easily combined with eyelid surgery.[3] The 2016 case series[5] and 2026 comparison[4] are described above. A 2016 review covers open brow lift surgery.[1]

timeline.event: Erich Lexer publishes the first documented discussion of a forehead lift.[9]
Chart review of endoscopic pretrichial brow lift published.[3]
Article on scalp advancement with pretrichial brow lift.[2]
